subject: Risk balance: pro-rata billing-cycle cap vs term-cumulative cap — framing for legal review
messages:
From: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>
To: Tom Jenkins <tjenkins@acme-corp.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-06-01T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Risk balance: pro-rata billing-cycle cap vs term-cumulative cap — framing for legal review

Tom — thanks for the call this morning. As discussed, ACME's procurement team pushed back on a single cumulative cap tied to total fees for the full term, and asked whether we can present a pro-rata, per-billing-cycle approach instead. I pulled together two concise framing options for legal to review and respond with company position (attached redlines and an XLS with numeric scenarios):

1) Per-billing-cycle (pro-rata) cap: cap resets each billing period (monthly/quarterly) and severity calculations are applied per invoice bucket. Practical when usage is highly variable and procurement wants narrower exposure windows. Pros: predictable annual exposure slices, easier to reconcile with invoices. Cons: aggregate recovery across term can exceed a single-term cap, creates potential stacking of exposures across extreme months.

2) Term-cumulative cap (single aggregate): cap equals a multiple of fees paid over the contract term (e.g., 1x fees paid during term or 3x fees in a 12-month rolling window). Pros: clear single-number exposure, easier for our actuarial modeling. Cons: may be a harder sell to procurement who are focused on short-term budget impact.

Key asks for legal:
- Which cap architecture is acceptable from a precedent and risk perspective?
- If we tolerate pro-rata windows, what contractual guardrails do we require to avoid runaway stacking (e.g., per-customer annual cap floor, cap on consecutive-period stacking, carveouts)?
- Preferred language for measuring "fees paid" (invoice basis vs recognized revenue) and whether we allow annual true-up / offset mechanics.

I've attached redlines (MSA_v3) with inline suggestions (see section 9 and defined term "Fees Paid"). Marissa will propose commercial-facing bullets for the counteroffer. Laura / Steph — tagging you for legal take.

Thanks,
Jonas
Director, GTM Strategy
Redwood Inference

Attachments:
- redlines_MSA_v3.docx (track changes, redline on Section 9: Limitation of Liability)
- orderform_cap_scenarios.xlsx (three numeric scenarios: 0.5x, 1x, 3x multiples; monthly vs annual windows)

Subject: Re: Risk balance: pro-rata billing-cycle cap vs term-cumulative cap — framing for legal review

Jonas — appreciate the writeup and options. Procurement's viewpoint in short: they want to avoid large single-event exposure rolling into future months (they worry about sustained outages driving multi-month charges). Their negotiation wish-list: a cap that limits quarterly/annual vendor exposure without leaving them undercompensated for catastrophic events.

Specific asks from ACME:
- Can Redwood do a quarterly reset with an annual aggregate floor (so per-quarter caps apply but there's an annual maximum that prevents unlimited stacking)?
- If the cap is measured as a multiple of fees, they prefer "fees invoiced" rather than recognized revenue.
- They want examples of numeric outcomes under our proposals (happy to review the XLS).

On legal language, their counsel will need to see a clean redline and a short one-page rationale we can share internally.

Tom
Head of Procurement, ACME Corp

Tom / team — looping back with a short commercial counterproposal and an explanation you can share with internal counsel. We've also uploaded a clean redline and an illustrative XLS to the shared Drive link.

Commercial counterproposal (high level):
- Primary structure: Quarterly-capped approach (cap = 1.5x fees invoiced in that quarter) to address procurement's desire to limit short-term exposure.
- Annual aggregate guardrail: an annual aggregate cap equal to 3x fees invoiced in the 12-month period (this prevents unlimited stacking across quarters).
- "Fees invoiced" is the measurement point (clear, ties to invoices).
- True-up: if a customer is billed retroactively (credit/adjustment), we allow a 60-day true-up window to correct the calculation.

Rationale for the hybrid: it balances ACME's short-term budget protection with Redwood's need for a bounded maximum exposure over the year. It also maps cleanly to invoicing systems for both sides.

Attached: clean_redline_MSA.docx (friendly language reflecting the above), and orderform_cap_scenarios.xlsx (with the quarterly/annual numbers filled).

Can legal confirm whether the hybrid wording has any downstream risk (e.g., ambiguous "stacking" interpretation or audit complexity)?

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Commercial Counsel (contracts partner)
Redwood Inference

From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com>

Date: 2028-06-02T16:20:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Risk balance: pro-rata billing-cycle cap vs term-cumulative cap — framing for legal review

Tom / team — thanks for the proposal and the example scenarios. From a legal/risk perspective, the hybrid (quarterly cap + annual aggregate guardrail) is workable provided we tighten a few drafting points. Below are redline-level bullets we will incorporate into the MSA: 

1) Defined term: "Fees Invoiced" — defined as gross invoiced amounts billed to Customer under the Order Form during the relevant period, net of refunds and unapplied credits. Avoid "recognized revenue" language.

2) Stacking language: include an explicit sentence that the annual aggregate cap is an absolute ceiling and that "stacking" across quarterly caps cannot result in recoveries above the annual aggregate cap. Example clause: "Notwithstanding the per-quarter cap, the total aggregate liability for all claims during any rolling 12-month period shall not exceed the Annual Aggregate Cap."

3) Calculation mechanics: require both parties to use mutually-agreed invoice exports as the source of truth; allow for a single dispute mechanism and a 60-day reconciliation period. This avoids open-ended "true-up" disputes.

4) Multiples and carveouts: we are comfortable with a 1.5x quarterly / 3x annual multiple if ACME agrees to standard carveouts (willful misconduct, IP indemnity, PCI/Soc2 data breaches where obligations caused by us). Carveouts should be enumerated and not open-ended.

5) Audit and complexity: include a clause limiting any audit scope to invoicing-related reconciliation for cap calculation and prohibit fishing expeditions into unrelated systems.

Next steps: Marissa will post a tracked-clean redline with the above language; I will add a brief memo (1 page) explaining the drafting choices for ACME procurement and counsel to attach to the redline. If ACME's counsel sends an initial counter-redline, please route it to contracts@redwood.com and cc me so we can accelerate a one-page response.

Best,
Stephanie Nguyen
Senior Counsel, Commercial & Privacy
Redwood Inference
